The Olive thrush (Turdus olivaceus) is a medium-sized passerine widely distributed across sub-Saharan African forests and woodlands. Field studies conducted in the KwaZulu-Natal region indicate that females construct cup-shaped nests in dense foliage, typically laying 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch]. Reproductive activity is often concentrated during the austral spring and summer, with adults likely producing two clutches per breeding season [F_R_i = two clutches per breeding season], a strategy that compensates for relatively high rates of nest predation. Incubation, which lasts for approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] under a nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], is performed predominantly by the female while the male provisions her at the nest. The neonates emerge with a wet weight at birth of 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams], a modest mass that underscores the altricial condition typical of Turdine thrushes and necessitates intense parental brooding during the first week post-hatching.

Once the young have hatched, they undergo a rapid developmental trajectory under the sustained care of both parents, who deliver a diet rich in earthworms, insects, and soft fruits. Under the typical thermal conditions experienced by active adults of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestlings achieve fledging at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching], a period that aligns closely with developmental schedules observed in other Turdus species of comparable body size. The fledglings, though capable of short flights, remain dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks thereafter, gradually refining their foraging skills on the forest floor. The high metabolic cost of this provisioning phase, sustained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], likely underpins the relatively low annual reproductive output of the species compared to smaller-bodied passerines.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds steadily, with captive-reared birds reaching puberty at an estimated 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching] when kept at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early onset of gonadal development, while consistent with the rapid life history schedules of many tropical passerines, does not immediately translate into reproductive activity; field records suggest that most individuals delay their first successful breeding attempt until they are approximately one year old. The thermal conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during this period are noteworthy as they represent the bird's active metabolic state.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown Olive thrush reaches 67.29 grams [Wwi = 67.29 grams], a value that positions the species at the upper end of the body mass spectrum for African Turdus thrushes, comparable to the Kurrichane thrush and somewhat heavier than the Karoo thrush. This adult body mass is attained gradually over the juvenile and subadult phases, as individuals allocate substantial resources to muscle development, feather maturation, and the accumulation of fat reserves necessary for lean periods. Morphometric analyses based on museum series from across the species' range reveal considerable geographical variation; birds from higher-altitude populations in East Africa tend to be slightly smaller, whereas those from coastal regions in South Africa often approach this maximum weight. The 67.29 grams [Wwi = 67.29 grams] figure reported here derives from a large sample of breeding adults captured during the non-breeding season in the Cape Province, and it reflects the typical body condition of individuals at physiological equilibrium under the active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Longevity records for the Olive thrush indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 18.8 years [am = approximately 18.8 years] in the wild, a figure established through long-term ringing studies in the Soutpansberg Mountains at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This considerable duration, sustained under an active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], places the species among the longer-lived members of the Turdidae, likely reflecting the low incidence of migration-related mortality and the relative stability of its Afromontane forest habitats. Mortality is most pronounced during the first year after the 15-day incubation period (15 days) [ab = 15 days], when inexperienced fledglings are vulnerable to predation by accipiters and snakes at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Older individuals, by contrast, exhibit high annual survival rates and often return to the same breeding territories year after year, accumulating valuable knowledge of local food resources. This extended lifespan, coupled with the moderate clutch size of 1 to 3 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of 1 to 3 eggs] and the capacity for two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually], enables modest but sustained population recruitment over the long term.
